pumac-2010-team-01.title: Centroid as centre of mass
pumac-2010-team-01.body:
The shape of the tetrahedron does not matter. With position vectors, $M=\frac{A+B+C+D}4$ and $N=\frac{B+C+D}3$, so $M=\frac14A+\frac34N$, i.e. $M$ lies on $AN$ with $AM=\frac34AN$. Hence $\frac{AN}{AM}=\frac43$, $p=4$, $q=3$, and the concatenation is $43$.

**Answer: 43**

pumac-2010-team-02.title: Pigeonhole
pumac-2010-team-02.body:
There are $13$ ranks, and (with $2010$ decks) plenty of cards of each rank. The worst case avoiding a four-of-a-kind is $3$ cards of each rank: $13\cdot3=39$ cards. The next card must complete a four-of-a-kind, so $k=40$. The number of decks does not matter. The last two digits are $40$.

**Answer: 40**

pumac-2010-team-04.title: Square and add
pumac-2010-team-04.body:
$(\cos a+\cos b)^2+(\sin a+\sin b)^2=2+2(\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b)=2+2\cos(a-b)$. The left side is $\frac{50}{29}+\frac{16}{29}=\frac{66}{29}$. So $2\cos(a-b)=\frac{66}{29}-2=\frac8{29}$ and $\cos(a-b)=\frac4{29}$, already in lowest terms. The concatenation is $429$.

**Answer: 429**

pumac-2010-team-05.title: Find when Tengyao pays
pumac-2010-team-05.body:
$R$ and $B$ are between $2$ and $12$, and $49=7^2$ divides $RB$ only if $7\mid R$ and $7\mid B$ (as $7$ is prime and no value from $2$ to $12$ other than $7$ is a multiple of $7$), i.e. $R=B=7$. Each pair of dice sums to $7$ with probability $\frac16$, so both do with probability $\frac1{36}$. The two coins match with probability $\frac12$. So Tengyao pays with probability $\frac1{72}$ and keeps his money with probability $\frac{71}{72}$. The concatenation of $71$ and $72$ is $7172$.

**Answer: 7172**

pumac-2010-team-06.title: Angle sum
pumac-2010-team-06.body:
The interior angles of a $45$-gon sum to $(45-2)\pi=43\pi$. If $43$ or more angles were greater than $\pi$, their sum alone would exceed $43\pi$ (and the other angles are positive), a contradiction. So at most $42$.

$42$ is attainable: take a triangle and replace one side by a chain of $42$ extra vertices bulging slightly into the triangle; this gives a $45$-gon with $42$ reflex angles and $3$ convex ones.

**Answer: 42**

pumac-2010-team-07.title: Set up the equal-probability condition
pumac-2010-team-07.body:
Suppose there are $c$ colours with $n$ balls each. The probability of two matching balls is $\dfrac{c\,n(n-1)}{cn(cn-1)}=\dfrac{n-1}{cn-1}$. After adding $k=20$ balls of a new colour it is $\dfrac{cn(n-1)+k(k-1)}{(cn+k)(cn+k-1)}$. Setting them equal and simplifying (most terms cancel) gives $c(k+1-2n)=k-1$, i.e. $c(21-2n)=19$. Since $19$ is prime, $21-2n\in\{1,19,-1,-19\}$ with $c>0$: $21-2n=1$ gives $c=19$, $n=10$; $21-2n=19$ gives $c=1$, $n=1$, which is impossible (with $n=1$ the original probability is $0$ but the new one is positive). So there were $19\cdot10=190$ balls, and after stealing one there are $189$.

**Answer: 189**

pumac-2010-team-08.title: Write an equation
pumac-2010-team-08.body:
Let the number be $x$. Putting $1$ in front gives $100000+x$, putting $1$ at the end gives $10x+1$. The condition is $3(100000+x)=10x+1$, so $7x=299999$ and $x=42857$. (Check: $142857\cdot3=428571$.)

**Answer: 42857**

pumac-2010-team-09.title: Factor 28 into five distinct integers
pumac-2010-team-09.body:
The numbers $8-a,\dots,8-e$ are five distinct integers with product $28=2^2\cdot7$. Let $k$ of them have absolute value $1$ (so $k\le2$, since only $1$ and $-1$ are available). The other $5-k$ have absolute value at least $2$ and their absolute values multiply to $28=2\cdot2\cdot7$, which has only three prime factors counted with multiplicity, so $5-k\le3$. Hence $k=2$, the values $1,-1$ occur, and the other three have absolute values $2,2,7$; being distinct they are $2,-2,7$. Their product is $1\cdot(-1)\cdot2\cdot(-2)\cdot7=28$. So $\{8-a,\dots,8-e\}=\{1,-1,2,-2,7\}$, whose sum is $7=40-(a+b+c+d+e)$. Hence $a+b+c+d+e=33$.

**Answer: 33**

pumac-2010-team-10.title: Force the first three seats
pumac-2010-team-10.body:
Gary wants an aisle seat but not $P1$, so Gary sits in $P7$. Charles also wants an aisle seat, so Charles sits in $P1$. Bob has exactly one seat between himself and Charles, so Bob sits in $P3$. The remaining four friends (Alex, David, Evan, Frankenstein) can fill $P2,P4,P5,P6$ in any order: $4!=24$ ways.

**Answer: 24**

pumac-2010-team-11.title: Search near the top
pumac-2010-team-11.body:
The digit sum of a number below $500000$ is at most $4+5\cdot9=49$, so the number must be close to $499999$: the square root must be near $707$. A number with digit sum $43$ is $\equiv7\pmod9$, and squares are $\equiv7\pmod9$ only for roots $\equiv4,5\pmod9$. Try $707\equiv5$: $707^2=499849$, with digit sum $4+9+9+8+4+9=43$. A computer check of all squares from $317^2$ to $707^2$ finds no other number with digit sum $43$.

**Answer: 499849**

pumac-2010-team-12.title: 29 as the shorter leg
pumac-2010-team-12.body:
The perimeter is largest when $29$ is a leg and the hypotenuse exceeds the other leg by $1$: $29^2+n^2=(n+1)^2$ gives $841=2n+1$, so $n=420$ and the hypotenuse is $421$ (perimeter $29+420+421=870$). In general, $29^2=(c-b)(c+b)$ with $29$ prime forces $(c-b,c+b)=(1,841)$, the only factorisation with $c+b>c-b$, so this is the only triangle with $29$ as a leg; with $29$ as hypotenuse the other sides are less than $29$, giving a smaller perimeter.

**Answer: 421**

pumac-2010-team-13.title: Construction and known lower bound
pumac-2010-team-13.body:
For $n\ge4$ dons the minimum number of calls is $2n-4$.

**Upper bound.** Pick four dons $a,b,c,d$. Each of the other $n-4$ dons calls $a$ ($n-4$ calls). Then $a,b,c,d$ make the calls $ab,\ cd,\ ac,\ bd$ (after $ab$ and $cd$, each pair shares its knowledge; after $ac$ and $bd$, all four know everything). Finally each of the $n-4$ outsiders calls one of the four again ($n-4$ calls). Total $2(n-4)+4=2n-4$.

**Lower bound.** That $2n-4$ calls are necessary is a classical theorem (Baker-Shostak; Hajnal-Milner-Szemeredi; see Bollobas, *The Art of Mathematics*), whose proof is longer than this problem warrants.

For $n=100$: $2\cdot100-4=196$.

**Answer: 196**
